trial_name: NONSEDA — Nonsedation vs Light Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated ICU Patients (2020)
citation: Olsen HT, Nedergaard HK, Strøm T, Oxlund J, Wian KA, Ytrebø LM, et al. Nonsedation or light sedation in critically ill, mechanically ventilated patients. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(12):1103-1111.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, investigator-initiated, pragmatic, parallel-group, open-label
one_liner: In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, a non-sedation strategy did not reduce 90-day mortality compared to light sedation and increased device-related adverse events.

pico.population: Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, screened within 24 hours of intubation, expected ventilation >24 hours
pico.intervention: Non-sedation strategy: no continuous sedative infusions, analgesia-first, rescue sedation as needed
pico.comparison: Light sedation strategy: protocolised sedation with daily wake-up trial, titrated to RASS -2 to -3

background.existing_knowledge: Deep or prolonged sedation is linked to delayed liberation, delirium, and longer ICU stays. Sedation minimisation strategies like daily interruption and bundled spontaneous awakening/breathing trials have been tested. A prior single-centre trial of a 'no sedation' protocol suggested potential resource outcome improvements but raised feasibility and safety questions.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a maximal de-escalation to 'no sedation' improves mortality and patient-centred outcomes compared to protocolised light sedation in modern ICUs was uncertain.
background.hypothesis: A protocol of non-sedation would reduce 90-day all-cause mortality compared with protocolised light sedation including a daily wake-up trial.

methods.design: Multicentre, investigator-initiated, pragmatic, parallel-group RCT with stratified randomisation (centre, age category, shock at admission).
methods.setting: 8 ICUs in Denmark, Norway, and Sweden.

exclusion: Conditions mandating continuous sedation or neurological control (e.g., therapeutic hypothermia, status epilepticus, elevated intracranial pressure/need for controlled ventilation)
Severe hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 9 kPa in the published protocol)

methods.intervention: Non-sedation strategy: No continuous sedative infusions; analgesia-first (typically opioid boluses/infusion per protocol) with environmental/comfort measures; sedation permitted as rescue (e.g., severe agitation threatening safety or ventilation synchrony). Target state: Awake or lightly sedated when feasible.
methods.comparison: Light sedation strategy: Protocolised sedation with daily wake-up trial; sedative choice per protocol (propofol initially, midazolam as needed), titrated to a light sedation target (RASS approximately -2 to -3) and interrupted daily when clinically appropriate.
methods.blinding: No blinding of treating clinicians or patients (behavioural intervention); mortality was objective and captured from registries/records.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned n≈700 to detect a 25% relative risk reduction in mortality with 80% power (β=0.20) at a two-sided 5% significance level (α=0.05).
secondary_outcomes: Days without mechanical ventilation within 28 days
Days free from coma or delirium within 28 days
Accidental self-extubation requiring re-intubation within 24 hours
Accidental removal of other equipment (e.g., lines/tubes)
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome at 90 days; key secondary outcomes assessed over 28 days and selected safety events during ICU stay.

headline_bullets: Non-sedation did not improve 90-day mortality (42.4% vs 37.0%; risk difference +5.4 percentage points; P=0.65).
Protocol separation was incomplete: mean RASS ranged from -1.3 to -0.8 (non-sedation) vs -2.3 to -1.8 (light sedation) over days 1-7.
Device-related harms were more frequent with non-sedation (e.g., re-intubation after self-extubation within 24 hours: 8.9% vs 4.0%; P=0.01).

outcomes_table.outcome: Days without mechanical ventilation within 28 days (median, IQR)
Days in ICU within 28 days (median, IQR)
Days free from coma or delirium within 28 days (median, IQR)
outcomes_table.note: Composite of coma and delirium assessments
Secondary outcome; interpret cautiously given multiple comparisons

outcomes_table.outcome: Accidental self-extubation requiring re-intubation within 24 hours
outcomes_table.note: Safety outcome from trial supplementary appendix

outcomes_table.outcome: Accidental removal of other equipment (e.g., lines/tubes)
outcomes_table.note: Safety outcome from trial supplementary appendix

safety: Accidental self-extubation requiring re-intubation within 24 hours: 8.9% non-sedation vs 4.0% light sedation (P=0.01)
Accidental removal of other equipment: 15.2% non-sedation vs 9.1% light sedation (P=0.01)

domains.notes: Centralised, concealed allocation with stratification by centre, age category, and shock at admission.

Open-label care; primary endpoint (all-cause mortality) is objective and less susceptible to ascertainment bias; several secondary outcomes (e.g., delirium assessments, adverse events) are more vulnerable to measurement and care-process differences.
710 randomised; 10 excluded from the modified ITT (5 per group); primary outcome ascertainment was otherwise complete via records/registries.

Clinical separation was measurable but imperfect; rescue sedation occurred in a substantial minority of the non-sedation arm (sedation within 24 hours: 27% non-sedation; any time during ICU stay: 38.4% non-sedation).
Groups were broadly comparable; small differences included APACHE II score (median 26 non-sedation vs 25 light sedation) and age (median 72 vs 70 years).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate: randomisation and follow-up for mortality were robust, but the necessarily unblinded design, incomplete separation (rescue sedation), and multiple secondary endpoints without multiplicity control complicate causal inference beyond the primary mortality outcome.

domains.notes: Mechanically ventilated adults in well-resourced Scandinavian ICUs (older median age ~70-72); patients with several conditions mandating deep sedation or neurological control were excluded.

Feasibility of non-sedation may depend on staffing and culture; participating ICUs reported high nurse:patient ratios and established protocols. Generalisability to ICUs with lower staffing, different delirium management practices, or different sedation norms may be limited.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is moderate for similar high-resource ICUs practising protocolised light sedation; translation to lower-resource or differently staffed settings is more uncertain.

limitations: Incomplete separation due to rescue sedation
Primary effect estimate compatible with benefit or harm
Multiple secondary outcomes increase false-positive risk

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted pragmatic trial with a robust primary endpoint, but the open-label design, incomplete protocol separation, and wide confidence intervals limit definitive conclusions about the non-inferiority or safety of a non-sedation strategy.
strengths: Multicentre, pragmatic design enhances real-world applicability
Objective primary outcome (90-day mortality) minimises detection bias
weaknesses: Unblinded design introduces potential for performance and detection bias in secondary outcomes
Frequent rescue sedation in the intervention arm dilutes the treatment contrast

sections.authors_conclusion: Compared with protocolised light sedation, routine non-sedation did not improve mortality and was associated with more device-related adverse events.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not support a routine non-sedation strategy for all mechanically ventilated patients and reinforces the current standard of an analgesia-first, light sedation approach.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Mechanically ventilated adults in well-resourced ICUs already using protocolised light sedation, excluding those with conditions mandating deep sedation.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That all sedation is harmful or should be avoided; the trial supports light, targeted sedation over no sedation.
implementation_caveats: Implementing a non-sedation strategy requires adequate staffing and established protocols for rescue sedation and managing device-related events.
The safety signal of increased self-extubation requires careful monitoring and preventative measures if sedation is minimised.

controversies.notes: The trial was designed to detect a large mortality effect; the observed CI still allows for smaller benefit or harm, meaning 'no difference' should be read as 'no evidence of a large benefit' rather than proof of equivalence.

controversies.topic: Exposure separation and pragmatic rescue sedation
controversies.notes: Rescue sedation was common in the non-sedation group, reflecting real-world feasibility constraints and potentially diluting treatment contrast.
Increased unplanned device-related events with non-sedation underscores the importance of staffing, mobilisation policies, delirium prevention, and rescue pathways when sedation is minimised.

unresolved_questions: Whether a non-sedation strategy could benefit specific subgroups not excluded from the trial.
The long-term functional and cognitive outcomes of survivors managed with different sedation strategies.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For most mechanically ventilated ICU patients, a strategy of analgesia-first light sedation is safer and as effective as a non-sedation strategy, which increases device-related harms.
